title: FAA tees up $875M AI tool to help manage air traffic congestion
content:
An AI tool is set to start advising air traffic controllers on managing air traffic in the congested airspace above the Washington, DC, area. The expected launch would be the first step toward a planned nationwide rollout covering the 29 million square miles of US national airspace overseen by the Federal Aviation Administration.
The FAA describes the SMART system as using AI models to predict air traffic flows and identify potential conflicts based on operational factors like airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, and airspace conditions. US government and industry officials told The Wall Street Journal that SMART could debut for the three major airports in the Washington, DC, area as soon as Monday, September 21.
The decision to launch SMART in a limited scope before going nationwide is the “right call,” said Philip Mann, principal consultant at Vector Strategic Consulting LLC, where he advises on aviation safety and AI governance. Mann previously worked at the FAA in multiple roles for 17 years.
“SMART’s risk was never any single prediction—it is a national-scale system with AI components carrying more unknowns than anything the FAA has fielded,” Mann wrote in an email to Ars. “Every cut in scope shrinks the unknowns.”
The AI-driven forecasts and recommendations are meant to give the FAA, airlines, and aircraft operators the same shared view of operational conditions so that they can agree on the most efficient routes and departure times. The goals of SMART include reducing aircraft fuel burn, improving on-time performance for flights, and speeding up recovery from weather and air traffic congestion events.
However, the airline industry was reportedly confused for weeks about the agency’s plans to deploy the AI tool, according to Politico. Anonymous airline officials told Politico that their concerns only eased after the FAA said the SMART AI tool would not change any procedures for air traffic controllers or airlines, and would instead produce “alternative route information” that is made available through existing FAA systems.

report.summary: FAA prepares to launch SMART, an $875M AI system that predicts air traffic conflicts, starting with Washington DC-area airports before a nationwide rollout.
report.background: The FAA has spent years trying to modernize a US air traffic system that handles tens of thousands of flights a day across 29 million square miles, where congestion, weather disruptions, and controller shortages regularly cause delays. Previous efforts, including the NextGen program, proved expensive and slow. SMART, estimated at $875 million, reflects a broader push to apply AI to operational aviation problems, following similar moves by airlines and other civil aviation authorities. The FAA is deliberately starting with the three major Washington, DC-area airports rather than deploying nationwide, a scope reduction that aviation safety experts say limits the system's unknowns while still generating real operational data before scaling up.
key_points: SMART uses AI models to predict air traffic flows and flag potential conflicts by combining airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, and airspace conditions. The goal is a shared operational picture for the FAA, airlines, and operators so they can agree on more efficient routes and departure times, reducing fuel burn and improving on-time performance.

The initial deployment covers the three major Washington, DC-area airports and could begin as soon as September 21. It is a limited-scope trial ahead of a planned nationwide rollout across the 29 million square miles of US national airspace overseen by the FAA.

Aviation safety consultant Philip Mann, who spent 17 years at the FAA, called the phased approach the 'right call.' He argued SMART's real risk is not any single prediction but the scale of a national AI system carrying more unknowns than anything the FAA has previously fielded.

Airlines were reportedly confused about the deployment for weeks, according to Politico. Their concerns eased only after the FAA said SMART would not change procedures for controllers or airlines and would instead provide 'alternative route information' through existing FAA systems.

At $875 million, SMART is one of the FAA's larger recent technology investments. Officials frame it as a decision-support tool rather than an automated controller, a distinction intended to keep human controllers responsible for safety-critical decisions.
report.impact: The launch is a significant test of AI in safety-critical public infrastructure. For the AI industry, it signals that governments will spend heavily on decision-support AI, but that deployments will be phased, tightly scoped, and judged on risk management rather than raw capability. For developers, SMART highlights demand for explainable, human-in-the-loop systems that integrate with legacy data pipelines and existing operational software. For regular travelers, the payoff is indirect but tangible: fewer weather- and congestion-driven delays, more efficient routings, and lower fuel burn. Success in Washington could accelerate AI adoption across the FAA; a high-profile failure could set back similar public-sector projects for years.
report.tools: Readers can explore open-source and public air traffic tools: BlueSky, an open-source air traffic management simulator from TU Delft for modeling traffic flows; the OpenSky Network for free ADS-B flight data; and NASA's FACET for air traffic simulation and analysis. FAA SWIM provides public system-wide information feeds, while FAA NextGen and SMART documentation pages offer official context on modernization plans.
